questions.question:
Consider the system of equations
\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
The value of \(x_3\) (round off to the nearest integer), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: A non-homogeneous system of 4 linear equations with 3 variables (\(x_1, x_2, x_3\)) represented as \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\):\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Aim: Solve for the value of \(x_3\) (rounded to the nearest integer).

3. Core Concepts:

System of Linear Equations: An overdetermined system (more equations than unknowns) has a unique solution if it is consistent and contains exactly 3 linearly independent equations.

Row Equivalency: Elementary row operations can eliminate redundant equations and isolate variables without altering the solution set.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Expand the matrix representation into standard algebraic equations.
  2. Scan for linear dependencies to eliminate redundant equations.
  3. Perform step-by-step substitution or subtraction to isolate \(x_3\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Write out the equations explicitly

  • Eq (1): \(x_1 + 3x_2 + 2x_3 = 1\)
  • Eq (2): \(2x_1 + 2x_2 - 3x_3 = 1\)
  • Eq (3): \(4x_1 + 4x_2 - 6x_3 = 2\)
  • Eq (4): \(2x_1 + 5x_2 + 2x_3 = 1\)

Step 2: Eliminate Redundancies

Observe that Eq (3) \(= 2 \times\) Eq (2), so Eq (3) is redundant and is dropped.

Step 3: Eliminate \(x_1\) — subtract Eq (2) from Eq (4)

\[(2x_1 + 5x_2 + 2x_3) - (2x_1 + 2x_2 - 3x_3) = 1 - 1 \]\[3x_2 + 5x_3 = 0 \implies x_2 = -\dfrac{5}{3}x_3 \]

Step 4: Express \(x_1\) in terms of \(x_3\) — substitute \(x_2\) into Eq (1):

\[x_1 + 3\left(-\dfrac{5}{3}x_3\right) + 2x_3 = 1 \implies x_1 = 1 + 3x_3 \]

Step 5: Solve for \(x_3\) — substitute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) into Eq (2):

\[2(1 + 3x_3) + 2\left(-\dfrac{5}{3}x_3\right) - 3x_3 = 1 \]\[2 + 6x_3 - \dfrac{10}{3}x_3 - 3x_3 = 1 \]\[\left(6 - \dfrac{10}{3} - 3\right)x_3 = -1 \]\[\left(\dfrac{9-10}{3}\right)x_3 = -1 \implies -\dfrac{1}{3}x_3 = -1 \implies x_3 = 3 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3 | Accepted key range: 3 to 3

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A rigid, uniform, weightless, horizontal bar is connected to three vertical members P, Q and R as shown in the figure (not drawn to the scale). All three members have identical axial stiffness of 10 kN/mm. The lower ends of bars P and R rest on a rigid horizontal surface. When NO load is applied, a gap of 2 mm exists between the lower end of the bar Q and the rigid horizontal surface. When a vertical load W is placed on the horizontal bar in the downward direction, the bar still remains horizontal and gets displaced by 5 mm in the vertically downward direction.



The magnitude of the load W (in kN, round off to the nearest integer), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Axial Force System

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Three identical vertical members: P, Q, and R.
    • Axial stiffness of each member: \(k = 10\) kN/mm.
    • Members P and R rest on a rigid base (no initial gap).
    • Member Q has an initial gap of \(\delta = 2\) mm above the base.
    • Under load \(W\), the rigid horizontal bar moves downward by \(\Delta = 5\) mm.
  • Aim: Determine the magnitude of the applied vertical load \(W\) (in kN).

3. Core Concepts:

Hooke's Law for Axial Bars: \(F = k \cdot \Delta l\), where \(k\) is the axial stiffness.

Compatibility Condition: Since the connecting top bar remains rigidly horizontal, the top ends of all three members displace downwards by exactly 5 mm.

Static Equilibrium:\[W = F_P + F_Q + F_R \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Deduce the effective compression (deformation) forced upon each member.
  2. Use stiffness to convert compressions into internal forces.
  3. Sum the forces to find the total applied load.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Determine Member Deformations

MemberTotal Displacement (mm)Initial Gap (mm)Effective Compression \(\Delta l\) (mm)
P505
Q52\(5 - 2 = 3\)
R505

Step 2: Calculate Internal Forces

\[F_P = 10 \times 5 = 50 \text{ kN} \]\[F_Q = 10 \times 3 = 30 \text{ kN} \]\[F_R = 10 \times 5 = 50 \text{ kN} \]

Step 3: Equilibrium Summation

\[W = F_P + F_Q + F_R = 50 + 30 + 50 = 130 \text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 130 kN | Accepted key range: 129 to 131

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question:
The flange and web plates of the doubly symmetric built-up section are connected by continuous 10 mm thick fillet welds as shown in the figure (not drawn to the scale). The moment of inertia of the section about its principal axis X-X is 7.73 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The permissible shear stress in the fillet welds is 100 N/mm². The design shear strength of the section is governed by the capacity of the fillet welds.



The maximum shear force (in kN, round off to one decimal place) that can be carried by the section, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Design of Steel Structures | Connections (Fillet Welds)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Cross-section: Built-up section with top/bottom flanges and two vertical web plates.
    • Flange dimensions: Width \(b = 100\) mm, Thickness \(t_f = 10\) mm.
    • Overall depth: \(D = 120\) mm.
    • Moment of inertia about NA: \(I_{xx} = 7.73 \times 10^6\) mm⁴.
    • Weld size: \(s = 10\) mm (continuous fillet welds).
    • Permissible weld shear stress: \(\tau_{vf} = 100\) N/mm².
    • Design criterion: Section capacity governed by fillet weld shear strength.
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum vertical shear force \(V\) (in kN) the built-up section can sustain.

3. Core Concepts:

Longitudinal Shear Flow (\(q\)): The horizontal shear force per unit length transferred between flange and web(s):\[q = \dfrac{V \cdot A\bar{y}}{I_{xx}} \]

Weld Shear Capacity (\(q_w\)): Total strength of continuous fillet welds per unit length:\[q_w = n \cdot t_e \cdot \tau_{vf} \]where \(n\) = number of continuous weld lines and \(t_e\) = effective throat thickness.

IS 800:2007 Provision: Effective throat thickness for standard 90° fusion welding: \(t_e = 0.7 \times s\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the number of weld lines \(n\) from the section diagram.
  2. Calculate effective throat thickness \(t_e\).
  3. Calculate the first moment of area (\(A\bar{y}\)) for the top flange about the neutral axis.
  4. Equate theoretical shear flow to total weld shear capacity and solve for \(V\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Weld Properties

  • Number of weld lines per flange: \(n = 4\) (each of the two web plates is welded on both inner and outer sides).
  • Effective throat thickness: \(t_e = 0.7 \times 10 = 7\) mm.
  • Total weld capacity per unit length:\[q_w = n \cdot t_e \cdot \tau_{vf} = 4 \times 7 \times 100 = 2800 \text{ N/mm} \]

Step 2: First Moment of Area (\(A\bar{y}\))

  • Area of top flange: \(A = 100 \times 10 = 1000\) mm².
  • Neutral axis at mid-depth: \(120 / 2 = 60\) mm from the top fiber.
  • Centroid of top flange: \(10/2 = 5\) mm from the top fiber.
  • Lever arm: \(\bar{y} = 60 - 5 = 55\) mm.\[A\bar{y} = 1000 \times 55 = 55000 \text{ mm}^3 \]

Step 3: Equate Shear Flow to Weld Capacity

\[\dfrac{V \cdot A\bar{y}}{I_{xx}} = q_w \]\[V = \dfrac{q_w \cdot I_{xx}}{A\bar{y}} = \dfrac{2800 \times 7.73 \times 10^6}{55000} \]\[V = 393527 \text{ N} \approx \mathbf{393.5 \text{ kN}} \]

Verification: Using \(t_e = 0.707 \times 10 = 7.07\) mm gives \(V \approx 397.4\) kN. Both values lie within the accepted GATE range, confirming the structural model of \(n = 4\) welds.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 393.5 kN | Accepted key range: 393.5 to 399.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question:
The singly reinforced concrete beam section shown in the figure (not drawn to the scale) is made of M25 grade concrete and Fe500 grade reinforcing steel. The total cross-sectional area of the tension steel is 942 mm².



As per Limit State Design of IS 456:2000, the design moment capacity (in kN.m, round off to two decimal places) of the beam section, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Cement Concrete | Limit State Design of Beams

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Width of beam: \(b = 300\) mm
    • Effective depth: \(d = 450\) mm
    • Area of tension steel: \(A_{st} = 942\) mm²
    • Concrete grade: M25 → \(f_{ck} = 25\) MPa
    • Steel grade: Fe500 → \(f_y = 500\) MPa
  • Aim: Calculate the design moment capacity \(M_u\) (in kN·m), rounded to two decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Depth of Actual Neutral Axis (\(x_u\)): Equating total compressive force to total tensile force (IS 456:2000, Annex G):\[C = T \implies 0.36\, f_{ck}\, b\, x_u = 0.87\, f_y\, A_{st} \]

Limiting Depth of Neutral Axis (\(x_{u,max}\)): For Fe500 steel (IS 456):\[x_{u,max} = 0.46\, d \]

Section Classification & Moment of Resistance: If \(x_u < x_{u,max}\), the section is under-reinforced (failure initiated by steel yielding):\[M_u = 0.87\, f_y\, A_{st}\,(d - 0.42\, x_u) \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the actual depth of the neutral axis (\(x_u\)).
  2. Compute the limiting depth (\(x_{u,max}\)) and compare to classify the section.
  3. Calculate the design moment capacity (\(M_u\)) using the appropriate lever arm.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Actual Depth of Neutral Axis (\(x_u\))

\[x_u = \dfrac{0.87\, f_y\, A_{st}}{0.36\, f_{ck}\, b} = \dfrac{0.87 \times 500 \times 942}{0.36 \times 25 \times 300} = \dfrac{409770}{2700} = 151.767 \text{ mm} \]

Step 2: Limiting Depth of Neutral Axis (\(x_{u,max}\))

\[x_{u,max} = 0.46 \times 450 = 207 \text{ mm} \]

Since \(x_u = 151.767\) mm \(< x_{u,max} = 207\) mm → Section is under-reinforced.

Step 3: Design Moment Capacity (\(M_u\))

\[M_u = 0.87\, f_y\, A_{st}\,(d - 0.42\, x_u) \]\[= 409770 \times (450 - 0.42 \times 151.767) \]\[= 409770 \times (450 - 63.742) \]\[= 409770 \times 386.258 \text{ N·mm} \]\[= 158{,}276{,}934 \text{ N·mm} = \mathbf{158.28 \text{ kN·m}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 158.28 kN·m | Accepted key range: 158.00 to 158.60

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: A simply supported prismatic concrete beam of rectangular cross-section, having a span of 8 m, is prestressed with an effective prestressing force of 600 kN. The eccentricity of the prestressing tendon is zero at supports and varies linearly to a value of e at the mid-span. In order to balance an external concentrated load of 12 kN applied at the mid-span, the required value of e (in mm, round off to the nearest integer) of the tendon, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Prestressed Concrete | Load Balancing Concept

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Span: \(L = 8\) m \(= 8000\) mm
    • Effective prestressing force: \(P = 600\) kN
    • Tendon profile: Linear (V-shaped) — eccentricity 0 at supports and \(e\) at mid-span.
    • External concentrated load at mid-span: \(W = 12\) kN
  • Aim: Find the eccentricity \(e\) (in mm) required to perfectly balance the external load \(W\).

3. Core Concepts:

Load Balancing Concept: A prestressing tendon with a sharp V-profile at mid-span creates an equivalent upward concentrated load \(W_p\) that counters external downward point loads:\[W_p = \dfrac{4Pe}{L} \]To balance the external load, set \(W_p = W\).

4. Solution Method:

Equate the equivalent upward prestress load to the external concentrated load and solve for the unknown eccentricity \(e\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Set up the load-balancing equation

\[W = \dfrac{4Pe}{L} \]

Step 2: Solve for \(e\)

\[12 = \dfrac{4 \times 600 \times e}{8000} = \dfrac{2400\,e}{8000} = 0.3\,e \]\[e = \dfrac{12}{0.3} = \mathbf{40 \text{ mm}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 40 mm | Accepted key range: 39 to 41

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Traffic volume count has been collected on a 2-lane road section which needs upgradation due to severe traffic flow condition. Maximum service flow rate per lane is observed as 1280 veh/h at level of service ‘C’. The Peak Hour Factor is reported as 0.78125. Historical traffic volume count provides Annual Average Daily Traffic as 12270 veh/day. Directional split of the traffic flow is observed to be 60:40. Assuming that traffic stream consists of ‘All Cars’ and all drivers are ‘Regular Commuters’, the number of extra lane(s) (round off to the next higher integer) to be provided, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Capacity

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Existing facility: 2-lane road
    • Maximum service flow rate per lane: \(c = 1280\) veh/h
    • Peak Hour Factor (PHF): \(0.78125\)
    • AADT: \(12270\) veh/day
    • Directional split: 60:40 (Major direction \(D = 0.60\))
    • Heavy vehicles adjustment factor: \(f_{HV} = 1.0\) (all cars)
    • Driver population factor: \(f_p = 1.0\) (regular commuters)
  • Aim: Find the number of extra lanes to be provided (rounded to next higher integer).

3. Core Concepts:

Correction Protocol: The K-factor (proportion of daily traffic in the peak hour) is missing. As per standard IRC/HCM practice for rural highways, K = 0.15 is assumed.

Directional Design Hourly Volume (DDHV):\[\text{DDHV} = \text{AADT} \times K \times D \]

Design Flow Rate (\(v_p\)):\[v_p = \dfrac{\text{DDHV}}{\text{PHF} \times f_{HV} \times f_p} \]

Number of Lanes (\(N\)):\[N = \dfrac{v_p}{c} \quad \text{(rounded up)} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Assume \(K = 0.15\) and calculate Peak Hour Volume (PHV).
  2. Calculate directional design flow rates for major (60%) and minor (40%) directions.
  3. Divide \(v_p\) by lane capacity and round up to get required lanes per direction.
  4. Subtract existing lanes (2) to find extra lanes needed.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Peak Hour Volume

\[\text{PHV} = 12270 \times 0.15 = 1840.5 \text{ veh/h} \]

Step 2: Directional Design Flow Rates

DirectionDDHV (veh/h)\(v_p\) (veh/h)
Major (60%)\(1840.5 \times 0.60 = 1104.3\)\(\dfrac{1104.3}{0.78125} = 1413.5\)
Minor (40%)\(1840.5 \times 0.40 = 736.2\)\(\dfrac{736.2}{0.78125} = 942.3\)

Step 3: Required Number of Lanes

Direction\(N = v_p / c\)Lanes Provided
Major\(1413.5 / 1280 = 1.104\)2
Minor\(942.3 / 1280 = 0.736\)1
Total Required3

Step 4: Extra Lanes

\[\text{Extra lanes} = 3 - 2 = \mathbf{1 \text{ lane}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1 extra lane | Accepted key range: 1 to 1

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A vertical retaining wall of 5 m height has to support soil having unit weight of 18 kN/m³, effective cohesion of 12 kN/m², and effective friction angle of 30°. As per Rankine’s earth pressure theory and assuming that a tension crack has occurred, the lateral active thrust on the wall per meter length (in kN/m, round off to two decimal places), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Earth Pressure Theories

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Height of wall: \(H = 5\) m
    • Unit weight of soil: \(\gamma = 18\) kN/m³
    • Effective cohesion: \(c' = 12\) kN/m²
    • Effective friction angle: \(\phi' = 30°\)
    • Theory: Rankine's earth pressure theory
    • Assumption: Tension crack has occurred
  • Aim: Lateral active thrust per meter length of wall (kN/m), rounded to two decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Coefficient of Active Earth Pressure (\(K_a\)):\[K_a = \dfrac{1 - \sin\phi'}{1 + \sin\phi'} \]

Depth of Tension Crack (\(z_c\)):\[z_c = \dfrac{2c'}{\gamma\sqrt{K_a}} \]

Lateral Active Thrust (\(P_a\)): Since tension crack has occurred, negative pressure in the zone 0 to \(z_c\) is completely ignored. Thrust is calculated from the positive triangular pressure distribution between \(z_c\) and \(H\):\[P_a = \dfrac{1}{2}\, K_a\, \gamma\, (H - z_c)^2 \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute active earth pressure coefficient (\(K_a\)).
  2. Compute theoretical depth of tension crack (\(z_c\)).
  3. Calculate lateral active thrust from the positive pressure triangle between \(z_c\) and \(H\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Active Earth Pressure Coefficient

\[K_a = \dfrac{1 - \sin 30°}{1 + \sin 30°} = \dfrac{1 - 0.5}{1 + 0.5} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.5} = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.333 \]

Step 2: Depth of Tension Crack

\[z_c = \dfrac{2 \times 12}{18 \times \sqrt{1/3}} = \dfrac{24}{18 \times 0.57735} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 2.309 \text{ m} \]

Step 3: Active Pressure at Base and Thrust

Active pressure at the base (\(z = H\)):

\[p_a(H) = K_a\,\gamma\,H - 2c'\sqrt{K_a} = \left(\dfrac{1}{3} \times 18 \times 5\right) - \left(2 \times 12 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \]\[= 30 - 13.856 = 16.144 \text{ kN/m}^2 \]

Lateral active thrust (area of positive pressure triangle from \(z_c\) to \(H\)):

\[P_a = \dfrac{1}{2} \times p_a(H) \times (H - z_c) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 16.144 \times (5 - 2.309) \]\[= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 16.144 \times 2.691 = \mathbf{21.72 \text{ kN/m}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 21.72 kN/m | Accepted key range: 21.00 to 22.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
Water flows in the upward direction in a tank through 2.5 m thick sand layer as shown in the figure. The void ratio and specific gravity of sand are 0.58 and 2.7, respectively. The sand is fully saturated. Unit weight of water is 10 kN/m³.



The effective stress (in kPa, round off to two decimal places) at point A, located 1 m above the base of tank, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Seepage & Effective Stress

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Upward flow of water in a tank.
    • Sand layer thickness: \(L = 2.5\) m
    • Void ratio: \(e = 0.58\)
    • Specific gravity: \(G = 2.7\)
    • \(\gamma_w = 10\) kN/m³ (saturated sand layer)
    • Point A is 1 m above the tank base → depth from top of sand: \(z_A = 2.5 - 1.0 = 1.5\) m
    • Seepage driving head: \(\Delta h = 1.2\) m
  • Aim: Effective stress at point A (\(\sigma'_A\)) in kPa, rounded to two decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Saturated and Submerged Unit Weight:\[\gamma_{sat} = \left(\dfrac{G + e}{1 + e}\right)\gamma_w \qquad \gamma' = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w \]

Hydraulic Gradient (\(i\)):\[i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L} \]

Effective Stress during Upward Flow: Seepage forces act upwards, reducing effective stress compared to static conditions.\[\sigma'_A = z_A\,(\gamma' - i\,\gamma_w) \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate submerged unit weight of sand (\(\gamma'\)).
  2. Calculate the hydraulic gradient driving upward flow (\(i\)).
  3. Calculate effective stress at depth \(z_A\) accounting for the opposing seepage gradient.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Saturated and Effective Unit Weights

\[\gamma_{sat} = \dfrac{2.7 + 0.58}{1 + 0.58} \times 10 = \dfrac{3.28}{1.58} \times 10 = 20.759 \text{ kN/m}^3 \]\[\gamma' = 20.759 - 10 = 10.759 \text{ kN/m}^3 \]

Step 2: Hydraulic Gradient

\[i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L} = \dfrac{1.2}{2.5} = 0.48 \]

Step 3: Effective Stress at Point A

\[\sigma'_A = z_A\,(\gamma' - i\,\gamma_w) = 1.5 \times (10.759 - 0.48 \times 10) \]\[= 1.5 \times (10.759 - 4.800) = 1.5 \times 5.959 = \mathbf{8.94 \text{ kPa}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 8.94 kPa | Accepted key range: 8.70 to 9.30

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A 10 m thick clay layer is resting over a 3 m thick sand layer and is submerged. A fill of 2 m thick sand with unit weight of 20 kN/m³ is placed above the clay layer to accelerate the rate of consolidation of the clay layer. Coefficient of consolidation of clay is 9×10⁻² m²/year and coefficient of volume compressibility of clay is 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ m²/kN. Assume Taylor’s relation between time factor and average degree of consolidation.



The settlement (in mm, round off to two decimal places) of the clay layer, 10 years after the construction of the fill, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Consolidation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Thickness of clay layer: \(H_{clay} = 10\) m
    • Thickness of sand fill: \(H_{fill} = 2\) m
    • Unit weight of sand fill: \(\gamma_{fill} = 20\) kN/m³
    • Coefficient of consolidation: \(c_v = 9 \times 10^{-2}\) m²/year
    • Coefficient of volume compressibility: \(m_v = 2.2 \times 10^{-4}\) m²/kN
    • Time elapsed: \(t = 10\) years
  • Aim: Settlement of the clay layer after 10 years (\(\Delta H_t\)) in mm.

3. Core Concepts:

Surcharge Loading: \(\Delta\sigma = \gamma_{fill} \times H_{fill}\)

Ultimate Consolidation Settlement: \(\Delta H = H_{clay} \cdot m_v \cdot \Delta\sigma\)

Drainage Condition: Sand fill above and sand layer below the clay → double drainage condition, so drainage path \(d = H_{clay}/2\).

Time Factor: \(T_v = \dfrac{c_v t}{d^2}\)

Degree of Consolidation (Taylor's relation for \(U \le 60\%\)): \(T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4} U^2\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Surcharge Load

\[\Delta\sigma = 20 \times 2 = 40 \text{ kN/m}^2 \]

Step 2: Ultimate Settlement

\[\Delta H = 10 \times 2.2 \times 10^{-4} \times 40 = 0.088 \text{ m} = 88 \text{ mm} \]

Step 3: Drainage Path (double drainage)

\[d = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5 \text{ m} \]

Step 4: Time Factor

\[T_v = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{-2} \times 10}{(5)^2} = \dfrac{0.9}{25} = 0.036 \]

Step 5: Average Degree of Consolidation

Since \(T_v = 0.036 < 0.282\) (boundary for \(U = 60\%\)), Taylor's relation applies:

\[0.036 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} U^2 \implies U = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.036 \times 4}{\pi}} = \sqrt{0.04584} = 0.2141 \quad (21.41\%) \]

Step 6: Settlement at 10 years

\[\Delta H_t = U \times \Delta H = 0.2141 \times 88 = \mathbf{18.84 \text{ mm}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 18.84 mm | Accepted key range: 18.50 to 19.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Three reservoirs P, Q, and R are interconnected by pipes as shown in the figure (not drawn to the scale). Piezometric head at the junction S of the pipes is 100 m. Assume acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/s² and density of water as 1000 kg/m³. The length of the pipe from junction S to the inlet of reservoir R is 180 m.



Considering head loss only due to friction (with friction factor of 0.03 for all the pipes), the height of water level in the lowermost reservoir R (in m, round off to one decimal place) with respect to the datum, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow & Networks

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Piezometric heads: \(H_P = 109\) m, \(H_Q = 106\) m, \(H_S = 100\) m
    • Pipes PS & QS: \(D_P = D_Q = 0.3\) m; Velocities: \(V_P = 2.56\) m/s, \(V_Q = 1.98\) m/s
    • Pipe SR: \(L_{SR} = 180\) m, \(D_R = 0.45\) m
    • Friction factor \(f = 0.03\), \(g = 9.81\) m/s²
  • Aim: Water level height in reservoir R (\(H_R\)), neglecting minor losses.

3. Core Concepts:

Continuity at Junction S: Since \(H_P, H_Q > H_S\), water flows from P and Q to S, then to R:\[Q_{SR} = Q_{PS} + Q_{QS} \]

Discharge: \(Q = \dfrac{\pi}{4} D^2 V\)

Darcy-Weisbach: \(h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD}\)

Energy Equation: \(H_R = H_S - h_{f,SR}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Discharges into S from P and Q

\[Q_{PS} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.3)^2 \times 2.56 = 0.18096 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[Q_{QS} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.3)^2 \times 1.98 = 0.13996 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

Step 2: Discharge and Velocity in SR

\[Q_{SR} = 0.18096 + 0.13996 = 0.32092 \text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[V_{SR} = \dfrac{0.32092}{\dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.45)^2} = \dfrac{0.32092}{0.15904} = 2.0178 \text{ m/s} \]

Step 3: Head Loss in SR

\[h_{f,SR} = \dfrac{0.03 \times 180 \times (2.0178)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.45} = \dfrac{5.4 \times 4.0715}{8.829} = 2.49 \text{ m} \]

Step 4: Water Level in Reservoir R

\[H_R = H_S - h_{f,SR} = 100 - 2.49 = \mathbf{97.51 \text{ m}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 97.5 m | Accepted key range: 97.2 to 97.8

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In a homogeneous unconfined aquifer of area 3.00 km², the water table was at an elevation of 102.00 m. After a natural recharge of volume 0.90 million cubic meter (Mm³), the water table rose to 103.20 m. After this recharge, ground water pumping took place and the water table dropped down to 101.20 m. The volume of ground water pumped after the natural recharge, expressed (in Mm³ and round off to two decimal places), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Groundwater Yield

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area: \(A = 3.00\) km² \(= 3 \times 10^6\) m²
    • Initial Water Table (WT) = 102.00 m
    • Recharge volume: \(V_{recharge} = 0.90\) Mm³ \(= 0.90 \times 10^6\) m³
    • WT after recharge = 103.20 m
    • WT after pumping = 101.20 m
  • Aim: Volume of groundwater pumped (\(V_{pumped}\)) in Mm³.

3. Core Concepts:

Specific Yield (\(S_y\)): Ratio of free-draining water volume to total bulk volume of the unconfined aquifer.

Volume Change Equation: \(\Delta V_{water} = S_y \times A \times \Delta h\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Determine Specific Yield (\(S_y\)) from recharge event

\[\Delta h_{rise} = 103.20 - 102.00 = 1.20 \text{ m} \]\[0.90 \times 10^6 = S_y \times 3 \times 10^6 \times 1.20 \implies S_y = \dfrac{0.90}{3.60} = 0.25 \]

Step 2: Calculate Volume Pumped

\[\Delta h_{drop} = 103.20 - 101.20 = 2.00 \text{ m} \]\[V_{pumped} = 0.25 \times 3 \times 10^6 \times 2.00 = 1.50 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^3 = \mathbf{1.50 \text{ Mm}^3} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.50 Mm³ | Accepted key range: 1.40 to 1.60

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A circular water tank of 2 m diameter has a circular orifice of diameter 0.1 m at the bottom. Water enters the tank steadily at a flow rate of 20 litre/s and escapes through the orifice. The coefficient of discharge of the orifice is 0.8. Consider the acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/s² and neglect frictional losses. The height of the water level (in m, round off to two decimal places) in the tank at the steady state, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Orifice Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Tank diameter: \(D = 2\) m (velocity of approach negligible)
    • Orifice diameter: \(d = 0.1\) m
    • Steady inflow rate: \(Q_{in} = 20\) L/s \(= 0.02\) m³/s
    • Coefficient of discharge: \(C_d = 0.8\)
  • Aim: Height of steady-state water level (\(H\)) in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

Steady State Principle: Water level is constant when inflow = outflow (\(Q_{in} = Q_{out}\)).

Orifice Discharge Formula: \(Q_{out} = C_d \cdot A_o \sqrt{2gH}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Orifice Area

\[A_o = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times (0.1)^2 = 0.007854 \text{ m}^2 \]

Step 2: Steady State Equation

\[0.02 = 0.8 \times 0.007854 \times \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times H} \]\[0.02 = 0.006283 \times 4.4294\,\sqrt{H} = 0.02783\,\sqrt{H} \]

Step 3: Solve for \(H\)

\[\sqrt{H} = \dfrac{0.02}{0.02783} = 0.7186 \]\[H = (0.7186)^2 = \mathbf{0.52 \text{ m}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.52 m | Accepted key range: 0.50 to 0.54

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) of a primary settling tank (discrete settling) is 20000 litre/m² per day. Kinematic viscosity of water in the tank is 1.01×10⁻² cm²/s. Specific gravity of the settling particles is 2.64. Acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s². The minimum diameter (in μm, round off to one decimal place) of the particles that will be removed with 80% efficiency in the tank, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Sedimentation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Surface Overflow Rate (SOR): \(V_c = 20000\) L/m²/day
    • Kinematic viscosity: \(\nu = 1.01 \times 10^{-2}\) cm²/s \(= 1.01 \times 10^{-6}\) m²/s
    • Specific gravity: \(G = 2.64\)
    • Target efficiency: \(\eta = 80\%\)
  • Aim: Minimum diameter of particles removed with 80% efficiency (in μm).

3. Core Concepts:

Discrete Settling Efficiency: \(\eta = \dfrac{V_s}{V_c} \times 100\%\), where \(V_s\) is the actual settling velocity.

Stokes' Law (laminar flow, \(Re < 1\)):\[V_s = \dfrac{g\,(G-1)\,d^2}{18\,\nu} \]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Convert SOR to m/s

\[V_c = \dfrac{20000 \times 10^{-3}}{1 \times 86400} = 2.3148 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Minimum Settling Velocity for 80% Efficiency

\[V_s = 0.80 \times 2.3148 \times 10^{-4} = 1.8518 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m/s} \]

Step 3: Particle Diameter from Stokes' Law

\[1.8518 \times 10^{-4} = \dfrac{9.81 \times (2.64-1) \times d^2}{18 \times 1.01 \times 10^{-6}} \]\[d^2 = \dfrac{1.8518 \times 10^{-4} \times 1.818 \times 10^{-5}}{16.0884} = 2.092 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}^2 \]\[d = \sqrt{2.092 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.446 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m} = \mathbf{14.5 \text{ μm}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 14.5 μm | Accepted key range: 14.0 to 15.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A gaseous chemical has a concentration of 41.6 μmol/m³ in air at 1 atm pressure and temperature 293 K. The universal gas constant R is 82.05×10⁻⁶ (m³ atm)/(mol K). Assuming that ideal gas law is valid, the concentration of the gaseous chemical (in ppm, round off to one decimal place), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Concentration = \(41.6\) μmol/m³
    • Pressure: \(P = 1\) atm
    • Temperature: \(T = 293\) K
    • Universal gas constant: \(R = 82.05 \times 10^{-6}\) m³·atm/(mol·K)
  • Aim: Find concentration in Parts Per Million (ppm).

3. Core Concepts:

Ideal Gas Law: \(PV = nRT\)

Volumetric PPM: For gaseous pollutants, 1 ppm = 1 μmol of pollutant per 1 mol of air.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Moles of Air per Cubic Meter

\[\dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{P}{RT} = \dfrac{1}{82.05 \times 10^{-6} \times 293} = \dfrac{1}{0.02404} = 41.597 \text{ mol/m}^3 \]

So 1 m³ of air contains 41.597 moles.

Step 2: Concentration in PPM

\[\text{ppm} = \dfrac{\text{moles of pollutant}}{\text{total moles of air}} = \dfrac{41.6 \text{ μmol}}{41.597 \text{ mol}} = 1.00007 \text{ μmol/mol} \approx \mathbf{1.0 \text{ ppm}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.0 ppm | Accepted key range: 0.9 to 1.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A stream with a flow rate of 5 m³/s is having an ultimate BOD of 30 mg/litre. A wastewater discharge of 0.20 m³/s having BOD₅ of 500 mg/litre joins the stream at a location and instantaneously gets mixed up completely. The cross-sectional area of the stream is 40 m² which remains constant. BOD exertion rate constant is 0.3 per day (logarithm base to e). The BOD (in mg/litre, round off to two decimal places) remaining at 3 km downstream from the mixing location, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Stream Deoxygenation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Stream: \(Q_s = 5\) m³/s, Ultimate BOD \(L_s = 30\) mg/L
    • Wastewater: \(Q_w = 0.20\) m³/s, 5-day BOD \(= 500\) mg/L
    • Stream cross-sectional area: \(A = 40\) m²
    • Target distance: \(D = 3\) km \(= 3000\) m
    • BOD rate constant: \(k = 0.3\) day⁻¹ (base e)
  • Aim: Ultimate BOD remaining (\(L_t\)) at 3 km downstream in mg/L.

3. Core Concepts:

First-Stage BOD Kinetics: \(BOD_t = L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) \implies L_0 = \dfrac{BOD_t}{1 - e^{-kt}}\)

Mass Balance at Discharge: \(L_{mix} = \dfrac{Q_s L_s + Q_w L_w}{Q_s + Q_w}\)

Remaining Ultimate BOD: \(L_t = L_{mix} \cdot e^{-kt}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Ultimate BOD of Wastewater (\(L_w\))

\[500 = L_w(1 - e^{-0.3 \times 5}) = L_w(1 - e^{-1.5}) = L_w \times 0.7769 \]\[L_w = \dfrac{500}{0.7769} = 643.61 \text{ mg/L} \]

Step 2: Mixed Stream Ultimate BOD (\(L_{mix}\))

\[L_{mix} = \dfrac{(5 \times 30) + (0.20 \times 643.61)}{5 + 0.20} = \dfrac{150 + 128.72}{5.20} = 53.60 \text{ mg/L} \]

Step 3: Travel Time to 3 km

\[v = \dfrac{Q_{mix}}{A} = \dfrac{5.20}{40} = 0.13 \text{ m/s} \]\[t_s = \dfrac{3000}{0.13} = 23076.9 \text{ s} \implies t = \dfrac{23076.9}{86400} = 0.2671 \text{ days} \]

Step 4: Ultimate BOD Remaining at 3 km

\[L_t = 53.60 \times e^{-0.3 \times 0.2671} = 53.60 \times e^{-0.08013} = 53.60 \times 0.9230 = \mathbf{49.47 \text{ mg/L}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 49.47 mg/L | Accepted key range: 49.00 to 50.00
